finalText:
**Merge** combines two branches by creating a new commit that has both as parents. It preserves history exactly as it happened—you can see when branches diverged and when they came back together.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history into a linear line. Cleaner to read, but it changes commit hashes, so never do it on branches others are using.

**When to use each:**

- **Merge**: Public/shared branches (main, release, anything pushed and shared). Also for intentional integration points you want to document ("we merged feature-X at this point").

- **Rebase**: Your own feature branch before pushing/merging. Cleans up messy local history (fixup commits, merge commits from pulling main) so the final PR is readable. Once pushed and shared, stop—rebasing breaks teammates' checkouts.

**Practical workflow**: While you're working locally on `feature-x`, rebase freely against `main` to keep it up-to-date. When it's ready to merge back, either merge it (most projects do this) or rebase one last time if your history is dirty, then merge. Don't force-push after others are using the branch.

The rule: rebase is a *local cleanup tool*; merge is how you *integrate*. Rebase writes cleaner logs, merge preserves truth.
